newsitem.title: USA: U.S. foils EU environment push at G7.
newsitem.headline: U.S. foils EU environment push at G7.

text.p: The United States has apparently foiled a European drive to have a Group of Seven summit call for clearly-defined cuts in the so-called greenhouse gases that lead to global warming, delegates said on Sunday.

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, a driving force behind a European Union initiative to cut carbon fuel emissions by 15 percent by the year 2010, said in an interview to be broadcast on German television that the summit "was split into two blocs, so to speak."
The United States, Japan and Canada did not support the EU proposal.
The final communique, due to be issued later on Sunday, was expected to call for significant cuts in emissions of carbon dioxide and other fuels but set no specific target, the delegates said.
"I think we'll succeed in finding a formula by Kyoto," Kohl told ZDF television, referring to a world climate conference in the Japanese city scheduled for December. "We have a few months' time."

The environment dispute produced one of the few points of discord at the Denver summit of the G7, the "rich men's club" of leading industrialised states that meets annually to set broad economic and political policy lines for the next year.

The EU leaders from Britain, France, Germany and Italy were keen to have the final communique set a clear target for greenhouse gas reductions before they attend a United Nations Earth Summit opening in New York on Monday.

Kohl told a closed-door summit session on Saturday that the environment was the most difficult issue at the summit and warned his partners their credibility would suffer if they did not agree a clear target for carbon emissions cuts.

French President Jacques Chirac was outspoken in his criticism of the U.S. position, saying: "There is a real divergence of views between, on one hand the Europeans and on the other the Americans -- not Canada, the United States."
Carbon dioxide and other so-called greenhouse gases are blamed for global warming and the climate change that results.
A special U.N. General Assembly session in New York next week will discuss progress in fighting global warming since the first Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro five years ago.
In contrast to greenhouse gases, the United States has pressed its G7 partners to agree to link export credit guarantees to a recipient country's record in protecting the environment.
German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said Bonn opposed this linkage and a group of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development would be asked to study the issue.
